data: The outermost of Uranus's major moons. Oberon's surface is heavily cratered and reddish-tinged — older than Titania's, with no clear evidence of resurfacing since the late heavy bombardment ~4 Gyr ago. Several large craters have notably dark floors; spectra are consistent with hydrocarbon residues left by space-weathered organics. A 6 km mountain — possibly the central peak of a large impact basin — rises near the limb in Voyager 2's best image.
Water-ice + silicate rock; reddish-tinged ancient cratered surface; the dark floors of several large craters are coated in unidentified dark material, possibly hydrocarbons or carbonates.
Oberon is the outermost of the five major Uranian moons (583,500 km orbit) — its surface is the most cratered, suggesting it has the oldest exposed surface in the Uranus system.
Galileo's four-night observation in 1610 ended geocentrism. The system's moons are still ending old assumptions today.
